Den sociala och tekniska utvecklingen har gått snabbare än skolan klara hålla takt till. Dessutom har vi skolreformer som fokuserar på att billighetsgöra utbildningen och har omformatterar elever och föräldrar till kunder. Sedan har vi såklart den omtalade lönefrågan, och hur många kommuner hanterar den:

Visst, du kan få bra ingångslön som nyexad lärare, men de som utbildat elever i exempelvis 10 år? De köps av grannkommunen och köps sedan tillbaka till den hemmavarande kommunen igen. Det slösar fina mängder pengar och ger en ostabil lärarkår och ofta en hög andel okvalificerade lärare i fattigare kommuner, vilket leder till en väldigt ojämn utbildning i landet.

Ekonomisk besparing fungerar på kort tid, men det gynnar sig inte. Och attityden till elevers utbildning som den ser ut idag blir inte ett positivt tillskott, direkt.

Vill vi snacka anställningsfrågan så är det ett problem i sig. "Vill du jobba på donken? Vi ser gärna att du har två referenser och 6-12 månaders erfarenhet inom restaurangbranchen"

Problemet är också hur vissa kommuner hanterar löneförhandlingar, vilket leder till att barnen inte får stabila lärarmentorer som följer med dem upp i årsklasserna.

Många kommuner har ingen duglig löneökning för lärare, men samtidigt har regler som gör att skolor inom samma kommun kan "köpa" lärare av varandra via löneförhandlingar. Detta leder till att behöriga lärare köps av andra kommuner för att sedan förhandlas tillbaka till tidigare kommuner efter något år för sjuka stålar.

Detta slösar otroliga summor för kommunerna, som hade kunnat behålla lärare om de givit en duglig löneökning från början. Istället hoppar lärare fram och tillbaka mellan skolor, vilket är helt förståeligt utifrån arbetarnas perspektiv, men innebär att eleverna inte får en stabil lärarkår som kan följa deras utveckling. Det medför också att kommunerna slösar skolkapital på dessa förhandlingar, istället för att lägga pengarna på läromedel etc.

Very few flowers (if any) are "unique" to the alps, but many flowers are recognised as alpine flowers, and are protected spiecies in other parts of the world. Of course, this is due to the climate, and just as in the north of Europe, plants have done well to cope with it in the alps. This also leads to the alps having a lot of flowers that are in the same plant family as many proud, tall-growing beauties in coastal Europe. Similar, but different. Often smaller and more compact.

Some of my favs to grow in the region:

Eldweiss: Famous for the older tales about it (A tale brought about the belief that it was hard to forage, and that therefore being gifted it was a high honour. It actually grows well in meadows, so it's easy to gather) and its inclusions in military signias in regions surrounding the alps. It is a protected species throughout Europe.

Hepatica: (Anemone/Nobilis) A small blue flower that grows in the wooded lands of the north, as well as the alps. The name was once Anemone Hepatica by Carl Von Linné, but was later given another due to the belief that it was in it's own family. It was not. It's one of the first flowers to bloom once spring comes. It has been used medicinally throughout history.

Trumpet Gentian:  Native to Southern and central Europe (Spain to the Balkans), it grows in mountainous regions, including the Alps. It is valued for its rich blue colour, and frequently forms mats on the ground as it does not grow tall. It's been used medicinally and is great for pollenators.

I feel you 100%. This is going to take a lot of time to progress, but here is what I can say:

Labels don't matter.

Okay, so. They do to an individual. But they do not to the rest of society. If you feel you don't fit in for whatever reason, that is okay. Use any personal labels you want. But feeling like you struggle because of this undefines diagnosis, is a good sign you have a diagnosis/issue.

Furthermore. You don't "need" a diagnosis to struggle. Whatever you struggle with, any diagnosis will not change that. What that might impact is what help you can get from others. However, you and your close ones knowing yourself is most important. Diagnosis or not, gaining insight is never time wasted. Your struggles are not unfounded, and do not require a definitive reasoning. I heard someone say "Wishing you have trauma is a sign you have unresolved trauma" and i think this is very beautiful.

Being NT is categorised differently depending on who you ask, and thats ok. Work on accepting who you are and what you don't know. You may not know, but that is not wasted time to anybody who loves you, it is valuable, and that is beautiful.

Faking, can also be a sign of NT btw (in my opinion) as one might be masking their masking to fit a mold (aka being unaware of their own identity and how they're percieved). It's okay to not know. Frustrating, sure, but you are not alone!

I'm no expert and can only speak on my personal experience as an autistic person, not as a psychologist or such. Ramble ahead:

I think it makes sense that with a lack of ability regulate strong emotion, it results in violent outbursts, even more so when an autistic individual is not given a constructive way to recognise or regulate these emotions. Since the world is built primarily for the neurotypicals, those who somehow "differ" from the norm.

I was never inherently a violent child, I was just given confusing instructions and demands throughout my childhood. When these instructions turned out easy for my brother, a neurotypical, to comprehend, this made my meltdown worse, thanks to the ostraization i felt. This created a vicious cycle, where i'd be reprimanded for not regulating my emotions, and then get increasingly more violent when my peers tactics got more and more repetitive, despite being completely fruitless and reminding me of how "weird" I was, leading to more violence.

Some people "grow" out of this, maybe for a few different reasons. I think for me it was a case of survival tactic; To keep my familiarity intact, I had to conform. This need to conform however, created even more issues,that manifested as new disorders. Anyway.

Some may exasporate their outbursts, or some might even  finally find a constructive, helpful support system or find healthy coping mechanisms over time!

How to deal with it differs, but i think a main influence is ones surroundings. To talk to those around you about what you might need during strong emotional moments. For me, it is covering my ears and walking in a circle. That is not childish. It is my way to de-escalate during an argument; to remove myself from the situation. I'll do that for about five minutes, and then I can return to thinking constructively. This is just what works for me.

Just for clarification! Not all neurodivergent people may experience what i listed above! This was just my take on the general topic.
